content.text:
Clear answer: **the fp8 lm head made each step slower** — it was not faster-but-dumber. Here's the disentanglement.

## Step time (the real effect)
| | fp8head (065) | baseline flex (066) |
|---|---|---|
| step_avg | **~170.5 ms** | **~161 ms** |
| steps in 300s | 1767 | 1878 |

fp8 head is ~**9–10 ms/step slower (~6%)**, so in the same 300s wall-clock budget it completes ~110 fewer steps.

## Per-step learning (essentially identical)
Train loss at matched steps — the curves overlap, fp8 is *not* learning worse:
| step | fp8head | baseline |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | 5.2621 | 5.2651 |
| 499 | 4.4052 | 4.4015 |
| 997 | 4.2563 | 4.2474 |

Differences are in the noise (±0.01), with the baseline a hair ahead.

## Why the final val loss looks worse
| | fp8head | baseline |
|---|---|---|
| final step reached | 1767 | 1878 |
| final val_loss | **3.8973** | **3.8667** |

The worse val loss at fixed wall-clock is **entirely a throughput effect**: fp8 got ~110 fewer steps in, not because each step learned less. Same loss-per-step, fewer steps → higher final loss.

## Bottom line
The fp8 lm head was a **regression on this hardware** — it slowed the step ~6% with no compute-quality benefit (per-step loss matched bf16). Whatever fp8 quantization/scaling overhead is being paid on the head's matmul isn't being recouped, likely because the head GEMM here isn't large enough (or the cast/scale overhead dominates) to benefit from fp8 tensor cores. I'd drop it unless you can get the head matmul fast path to actually trigger.

Note: logs 063 (flexbase) and 064 (first fp8head attempt) only have 1 and 0 logged steps respectively — they appear to have died at startup, so the valid comparison is 065 vs 066.
